newsitem.title: SPAIN: Three convicted for plotting to kill Spain's king.
newsitem.headline: Three convicted for plotting to kill Spain's king.

text.p: Spain's high court sentenced three suspected Basque separatist guerrillas to a total of 109 years in prison for plotting to kill King Juan Carlos in 1995, court officials said on Monday.
The court handed down prison sentences on Juan Jose Rego, Jorge Garcia and Ignacio Rego for crimes against the Crown and belonging to an armed band.
The trial attracted widespread interest among Spaniards when it started in Madrid on January 22.

In dramatic testimony, two of the three men charged -- Juan Jose Rego and Garcia -- related how they rented a flat on the Mediterranean island of Mallorca with a direct line of vision to the king's sailing yacht and how they had him in their rifle sights three times.
Garcia told the court he had not shot the king because escape plans had not yet been finalised.

He and Juan Jose Rego described King Juan Carlos, Crown Prince Felipe and Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar as "prime targets" for ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), which has killed 800 people in a nearly 30-year struggle for Basque independence.
The conviction came a week after the separatist rebels kidnapped and killed a young politician, sparking national outrage.

In the wake of the killing and the massive street protests that surrounded it, the government promised to speed up trials of ETA suspects and make legislative reforms to close legal loopholes exploited by the guerrillas.
But Spain's Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said the timing of the court's announcement on Monday was coincidental.
"It's wrong to think that this is a strategy by the separate state powers, because they maintain their independence," he told reporters.
The three men were each sentenced to 10 years prison for crimes against the Crown, eight for belonging to an armed band, eight for terrorism with arms of war, and eight for terrorism with explosives.
They also received one- and three-year sentences for forging official documents.
